title: SASLprep validates a UTF-8 sequence by its declared length without checking how many bytes remain
live_proof: inspection at the 17.5 pin. saslprep.c:1013-1022 is the validation loop: `while (*p) { l = pg_utf_mblen(p); if (!pg_utf8_islegal(p, l)) return -1; p += l; }`. pg_utf_mblen reads only the LEAD byte and returns the length that byte declares, up to 4. pg_utf8_islegal is then handed that l and reads l bytes. When the string's terminating NUL falls inside the declared sequence -- a truncated multibyte character at the end of the input -- the read runs past the NUL and past the end of the allocation, by up to three bytes. The loop condition `while (*p)` cannot prevent it because it is checked only at the lead byte. Upstream replaces the condition with a remaining-length counter and adds `len < l ||` in front of the islegal test; neither is present at the pin. saslprep.c:48 defines ALLOC as malloc under FRONTEND, so in libpq the string being walked is a libc allocation.
object: the NUL-terminated password string passed to pg_saslprep, a libc allocation in the client
lifetime_ender: n/a -- the object is live; the defect is a read past its end
shape: a declared multibyte length is trusted over the bytes actually remaining
fidelity: real function, real input, REPRODUCED. The reduction calls the real pg_utf8_string_len with the real pg_utf_mblen and pg_utf8_islegal, all three copied verbatim from the pin, on a malloc'd string whose last character is a truncated multibyte sequence -- exactly what libpq's scram_init passes when the application supplies such a password. No server is needed: the overread happens in the client before any byte goes on the wire.

spatial.oracle: the overrun of the malloc'd object is reported as a domain fault, or the case completes and this arm did not see it. level0 narrows a returned pointer to the bytes requested, not to a size class, so unlike the purecap guest the bound here is the object itself; the host's fault line carries the pc, and the expect_fault_in line the case prints before the defect is what attributes it.

cheribsd-revocation.oracle: completes with no capability fault -- REACHED-SILENT (CheriBSD riscv64-purecap, static build, 2026-10-06). The PG_DEFECT marker printed, so the overread provably executed. The reason the arm is silent was MEASURED rather than inferred: a probe calling cheri_length_get() on this guest's malloc shows the bounds are rounded to a size class, not to the request -- malloc(4) returns a capability of length 16, so the object has 12 bytes of slack and a one-byte overread never leaves the capability. Requested/granted pairs measured: 1->16, 4->16, 8->16, 16->16, 24->32, 32->32, 100->112, 400->448, 4096->4096. This is a limit of the mechanism's granularity for small objects, and it is independent of nesting: the object here came straight from libc. The fault handler installed for this run did not fire at all, which is the same statement as REACHED-SILENT made from the other side: the arm had a handler ready to attribute a fault and there was no fault to attribute.

host-asan.oracle: AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflow, READ of size 1, "0 bytes to the right of 4-byte region", in pg_utf8_islegal (shared/upstream_saslprep.c:45, the `a = source[2]` arm) called from pg_utf8_string_len (:96) from case.c:38. The 4-byte region is the malloc'd password "pw\xE2" with its terminator, so the overread is exactly one byte past the allocation -- pg_utf_mblen returned 3 for the 0xE2 at offset 2. Host build, 2026-10-06.

status: measured on all three arms 2026-10-06: spatial=detected, sublet=detected, cheribsd-revocation=silent
nested_why: The object comes straight from libc malloc. Nothing carves it out of a larger block, so it is not nested. libpq does have a nested allocator of its own, pqResultAlloc's PGresult blocks, but none of these five touches that storage.
